For counts, the natural model is a Poisson log-linear trend: log E[y] = a + b * t, so exp(b) is the rate ratio per period, the multiplicative change from one period to the next. cnttrnd() fits it with an interval:

set.seed(3)
y <- stats::rpois(8, lambda = 200 * 0.85^(0:7))   # falling ~15% a year
fit <- cnttrnd(y)
round(fit$rateratio, 3)
#> [1] 0.869

With a varying denominator the trend is in the rate, via an offset:

cnttrnd(c(20, 25, 30), offset = c(1000, 1500, 2500))$rateratio
#> [1] 0.7708656

Counts here rise while the rate per 1,000 falls, which is the finding.

A step change

A trend test asks “is it drifting?”; a step-change test asks “did it jump once?”. The best single split point is found by maximising the between-segment difference, and its significance is judged by permutation, which accounts for having searched over every possible split:

stepchg(c(100, 104, 98, 60, 63, 58))
#> $breakafter
#> [1] 3
#> 
#> $index
#> [1] 3
#> 
#> $before
#> [1] 100.6667
#> 
#> $after
#> [1] 60.33333
#> 
#> $difference
#> [1] -40.33333
#> 
#> $statistic
#> [1] 2440.167
#> 
#> $p_value
#> [1] 0.1
#> 
#> $nperm
#> [1] 720
#> 
#> $method
#> [1] "exact over all 720 orderings"

Pure noise still yields a best split, and it is not significant:

set.seed(2)
stepchg(stats::rnorm(12))$p_value
#> [1] 0.6223

Two survey periods

Survey tables often give only two periods, each with its confidence interval. The change between them has an interval of its own. healchg() gives it for every group and indicator at once. It lists wellness indicators first, reading change as Indigenous scholars of mental health read it, as a process of healing (Stewart 2008). Perceived mental health of adults, 2015/2018 and 2019/2022, by Statistics Canada (table 13-10-0924-01):

h <- indiex("health")
h <- h[h$age == "Total, 18 years and over" &
         h$indicator == "Perceived mental health, very good or excellent", ]
healchg(h, "group", "indicator", "period", "estimate", "lower", "upper",
               from = "2015/2018", to = "2019/2022", qual = "quality")
#>            group                                       indicator side from   to
#> 1  First Nations Perceived mental health, very good or excellent <NA> 59.8 45.8
#> 2          Métis Perceived mental health, very good or excellent <NA> 61.0 52.8
#> 3          Inuit Perceived mental health, very good or excellent <NA> 49.1 47.8
#> 4 Non-Indigenous Perceived mental health, very good or excellent <NA> 70.6 61.5
#>   change      lower      upper usewithcau
#> 1  -14.0 -17.687818 -10.312182      FALSE
#> 2   -8.2 -11.925923  -4.474077      FALSE
#> 3   -1.3  -9.974243   7.374243      FALSE
#> 4   -9.1  -9.702080  -8.497920      FALSE

A pace, projected

Some counts accumulate toward a fixed number: the 94 Calls to Action of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, for instance. trcprog() takes the pace so far as a Poisson rate with its exact interval, and gives the year all would be complete at that pace. That is a description of the pace, not a forecast.

trcprog()
#>   completed remaining years     rate    ratelo   rateup   cmplby cmplbyearly
#> 1        13        81  7.04 1.846591 0.9832319 3.157727 2066.865    2048.651
#>   cmplbylate
#> 1   2105.381

Choosing between them

Question Tool Reports
Is the series moving in one direction? trndtst() Mann–Kendall p-value, Sen’s slope with interval
By what factor per period? cnttrnd() rate ratio with interval, optional offset
Did it change once, and when? stepchg() split point, segment means, permutation p-value
Year over year, with publication rounding yoy() (its own vignette) exact intervals on each change

All of them work on the five to ten values a published table gives, and none of them assumes the counts are large.

The trend in a picture

plot() draws the counts with the fitted trend.

plot(fit)

References

Mann (1945). Nonparametric tests against trend. Econometrica 13(3). Kendall (1975). Rank Correlation Methods. 4th ed. Sen (1968). Estimates of the regression coefficient based on Kendall’s tau. JASA 63(324).

Plotting results

Every result the package returns draws itself. plot(x) needs nothing but the object; the chart is the one that result calls for, drawn with base graphics (no new dependency), with one shared look across the package. Every method takes the same customisation, and every method returns the numbers it drew, so a figure can be checked or redrawn another way.

One call per result

Stock and flow after Lakner (1976): the average daily population and the length of stay, one panel per measure.

sf <- stkflow(days = c(13500, 14600, 15100, 14200), people = c(300, 320, 310, 290),
                 prd = 2020:2023)
plot(sf)

Period-over-period change with its interval, coloured by verdict:

y <- yoy(data.frame(year = 2018:2023, n = c(40, 44, 41, 55, 52, 61)), value = "n",
         prd = "year")
plot(y)

Small counts get their percentages too: each comes with its exact interval, as wide as the base is small. Only a zero base has no percentage, and its row says so.

plot(yoy(data.frame(year = 2019:2023, n = c(10, 12, 11, 15, 14)), value = "n", prd = "year"))

Rates with their intervals, and the change in a rate:

d <- data.frame(division = rep(c("north", "east", "west"), 2), year = rep(2022:2023, each = 3),
                stops = c(120, 90, 60, 150, 85, 70), residents = c(1e4, 8e3, 5e3, 1e4, 8e3, 5e3))
plot(rtcalc(d[d$year == 2023, ], count = "stops", pop = "residents", by = "division"))

plot(ratechg(d, count = "stops", pop = "residents", prd = "year", by = "division"))

First digits against Benford’s law, the power curve of a check, and a permutation null:

set.seed(1)
amounts <- round(exp(rnorm(400, 6, 1.4)))
plot(benfordtst(amounts))

dd <- data.frame(x = rnorm(120), y = rnorm(120))
shift <- function(z, s) {
  z$y <- z$y + s * z$x
  z
}
plot(cpspwr(dd, function(z) cor(z$x, z$y), inject = shift, trt = "x",
                   sizes = c(0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6), n = 49, reps = 6, seed = 1))

Air pollution

The concentration-response curve with the exposure marked, the burden it implies, and the whole vrfpol() report on one page (curve, burden and the concentration curve of exposure over income):

plot(crfno2(25))

plot(polbrdn(25, 1, 0.008, 1e6, poll = "NO2"))

plot(vrfpol("no2", demo = TRUE))

A plume on a grid, and the particle cloud of the random walk:

plot(plmfld(q = 100, u = 5, h = 50, x = seq(100, 3000, by = 100),
                 y = seq(-500, 500, by = 50)))

plot(lagrprt(500, 0, 0, u = 2, v = 0.5, kx = 1, ky = 1, dt = 1, nsteps = 60,
                          grid = c(0, 200, -60, 100, 40, 32)))

The footprint of a computation: CPU, memory and the total in one unit chosen to fit, with its everyday equivalents under the bars:

plot(co2fp(for (i in 1:20) sum(sqrt(seq_len(2e5))), loc = "CA",
                       cpupwrw = 45, memgb = 8))

Courts and crime

The Ontario Court of Justice and Toronto Police Service data shipped with the package (see vignette("applied-analyses") for the analysis behind each one):

ext <- function(f) read.csv(system.file("extdata", f, package = "rmoriebricklayer"))
f <- ext("ocj_flow_ontario.csv")
d <- ext("ocj_time_to_disposition.csv")
x <- ext("ocj_dispositions.csv")
g <- ext("ocj_offence_groups.csv")
g <- g[g$year %in% c(2014, 2022), ]
b <- ext("tps_break_enter_d14_2024.csv")
b <- b[!is.na(b$lon), ]

Cases received and disposed, and the clearance rate:

plot(caseflow(f$received, f$disposed, pend = f$pending, prd = f$month))

How long cases stay open, from the published time-to-disposition bands:

last <- nrow(d)
plot(lifetbl(c(0, 10, 15, 18, Inf), unlist(d[last, 2:5]) * f$disposed[last]))

The mix of outcomes over the years:

plot(dispmix(x[, -(1:2)], prd = x$year))

A Simpson’s-paradox check: the parts’ rates, where the work moved, and the change split into rate and mix effects:

plot(clrdcmp(g$disposed, g$received, g$offence_group, g$year))

Where break-and-enters cluster, and whether they repeat near each other soon after:

plot(crmdens(b$lon, b$lat, ngrid = 120))

plot(knoxtst(b$lon, b$lat, as.Date(b$occ_date), c(100, 200, 400), c(7, 14, 28),
               nsim = 99, seed = 1))

First Nations, Metis and Inuit health

Published Statistics Canada estimates bundled with the package (?indiex; see vignette("applied-analyses") for the methods and the governance behind them). Each group is drawn on its own: the plots never pool First Nations, Metis and Inuit.

h <- indiex("health")
adults <- h[h$age == "Total, 18 years and over", ]
mh <- adults[adults$period == "2019/2022" & adults$indicator == "Perceived mental health, very good or excellent", ]

Each group against non-Indigenous adults, with intervals from the published ones:

plot(indgap(mh, "group", "estimate", "lower", "upper", qual = "quality"))

Perceived mental health on its whole scale (2022 Indigenous Peoples Survey):

r <- indiex("mentalhealth")
r <- r[r$region == "Canada", ]
plot(ordcmp(r, "group", "rating", "estimate", "lower", "upper",
                     lvls = c("Fair or poor", "Good", "Very good", "Excellent"),
                     ref = "M\u00e9tis", qual = "quality"))

Wellness beside distress, and the two as separate axes (2024 well-being table):

wb <- indiex("wellbeing")
w <- welprof(wb, "group", "indicator", "estimate", "lower", "upper",
                      well = c("Always or often has a hopeful outlook",
                                   "Sense of meaning and purpose rating of 8, 9 or 10"),
                      distress = c("Rarely or never has a hopeful outlook",
                                   "Life satisfaction rating between 0 and 5"),
                      qual = "quality")
plot(w)

plot(dualcont(w, "Always or often has a hopeful outlook", "Life satisfaction rating between 0 and 5"))

Change between the two survey periods, wellness first:

hc <- healchg(adults[adults$indicator %in% c("Perceived mental health, very good or excellent",
                                                    "Mood disorder"), ],
                     "group", "indicator", "period", "estimate", "lower", "upper",
                     from = "2015/2018", to = "2019/2022", qual = "quality",
                     well = "Perceived mental health, very good or excellent")
plot(hc)

The Truth and Reconciliation Commission’s Calls to Action, completed and projected:

plot(trcprog())

Evaluating a policy

The designs of vignette("statistical-methods"), on its made-up panel of twenty districts where a reform arrives in three stages: the outcome by adoption cohort before any model, the event study, the Goodman-Bacon weights behind a two-way fixed-effects estimate, and the randomisation null of the assignment.

p <- polex()
plot(cohtrnd(p, "district", "month", "crmrate", "refmonth", win = c(-10, 10)))

es <- evstudy(p, "district", "month", "crmrate", "refmonth", leads = 4, lags = 6)
plot(es)

plot(bacondcmp(p, "district", "month", "crmrate", "reformed"))

plot(perminf(p, "district", "month", "crmrate", "refmonth", cl = "region"))

Whether one district drives the estimate, and a single treated place against its synthetic control and its synthetic difference in differences:

plot(loounit(p, "district", "month", "crmrate", "reformed"))

p13 <- p[is.na(p$refmonth) | p$district == "D13", ]
plot(synctl(p13, "district", "month", "crmrate", "D13", adopt = 13))

plot(syndid(p13, "district", "month", "crmrate", "refmonth", reps = 50, seed = 1))

The power of the design on the untreated data, and the cross-fitted AIPW estimate of vignette("statistical-methods") with its overlap and balance checks:

plot(plnpwr(p[p$month <= 12, ], "district", "month", "crmrate", ntrt = 10, adopt = 7:10,
            eff = c(0, 0.5, 1, 1.5), reps = 40, seed = 1))

set.seed(7)
n <- 600
d <- data.frame(age = runif(n, 18, 70), income = rnorm(n))
d$t <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-2 + 0.04 * d$age + 0.5 * d$income))
d$y <- 10 + 3 * d$t + 0.2 * d$age + d$income + rnorm(n)
fit <- aipwcf(d, "y", "t", c("age", "income"), lrn = "ols")
plot(fit)

plot(fit, type = "estimate")

e <- pmin(pmax(attr(fit, "propensity")$propensity, 0.01), 0.99)
d$ipw <- ifelse(d$t == 1, 1 / e, 1 / (1 - e))
plot(baltab(d, "t", c("age", "income")), after = baltab(d, "t", c("age", "income"), w = "ipw"))

Customising

Every method takes main, col (or a palette name), grid, and ... for the base-graphics call. plotopt() sets the session defaults; blpal() gives the colour-blind-safe sets the package uses.

plot(sf, what = "alos", col = "firebrick", main = "Length of stay (days)", lwd = 3)

old <- plotopt(palette = "grey", grid = FALSE)
plot(y, what = "value")

plotopt(palette = old$palette, grid = old$grid)
blpal("okabe", 4)
#> [1] "#0072B2" "#D55E00" "#009E73" "#E69F00"

Every method returns the data it drew, invisibly:

drawn <- plot(y)

head(drawn, 3)
#>   label    pctchg     lower    upper verdict   at
#> 1  2018        NA        NA       NA    <NA> 2018
#> 2  2019 10.000000 -29.95683 73.20735      up 2019
#> 3  2020 -6.818182 -40.61975 45.94265    down 2020

Results that are plain data frames have a plot function of their own: the Lorenz curve of a vector, and the funnel plot of observed against expected counts per area.

plotlrnz(c(1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21))

plotfnl(obs = c(4, 20, 50, 9, 31), expd = c(5, 22, 40, 20, 30),
            area = c("a", "b", "c", "d", "e"))
